opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most important questions for the web right now, and I don't think anyone has the full answer yet.

The basic bargain of the web for the last twenty-five years has been pretty simple: someone creates content, a human comes to look at it, and somewhere along the way that human's attention gets monetized, mostly through ads. That bargain assumes the consumer of the page is a person with eyeballs. When an agent is doing the browsing, reading fifty pages in a few seconds to answer a question or complete a task, that assumption breaks. The agent doesn't see the banner, doesn't click the sponsored link, and doesn't come back tomorrow because it liked the site.

So if you just let things play out with no change, the people creating the content the agents depend on get squeezed. Their traffic, or at least their monetizable traffic, goes down while their content is being used more. That's not sustainable. If the incentive to publish high-quality information on the open web erodes, the agents themselves get worse, because they're only as good as what they can read.

I see a few things happening. First, some of the economic exchange has to move from attention to access. Instead of "I'll show you an ad," it becomes "this agent, or the person or company behind it, pays to use this content," whether that's per request, through licensing, or through some marketplace-style mechanism. The web was built on a free-plus-ads model partly because micropayments never worked for humans; the friction was too high. For machines that friction mostly goes away, so models that failed for people might actually work for agents.

Second, I think the web gets a second audience. For a long time we designed pages for humans and then did SEO for search crawlers. Now there's a third consumer: agents that want clean, structured, trustworthy information they can act on. Publishers and businesses will increasingly think about how they show up for agents, and that's both a risk and an opportunity.

Third, advertising doesn't disappear; it changes shape. When an agent is helping someone buy something or choose a service, there will be pressure to influence that decision. The big open question is whether that influence is transparent, so the user knows what's paid and what's organic, or whether it gets baked invisibly into agent recommendations. I think trust is going to be the scarce resource. If people can't trust their agents to act in their interest, the whole thing falls apart.

My overall view is that the web has to evolve so that agents are first-class participants, and that includes the economics, not just the technology. Done well, it could be a healthier web: creators get paid more directly for the value of what they produce, rather than for how many ads they can put in front of someone. Done badly, we end up with a web where content creation dries up and everything is mediated by a few closed systems. That's a big part of why I think it matters to build infrastructure for agents on the open web now, while these norms are still being set.

r001.rationale: The response describes ads monetizing human attention, but does not identify advertising as a mechanism for differential pricing.

r002.rationale: It explains that the ad model assumes a human with attention and that agents reading pages do not see banners or click sponsored links.

r003.rationale: It discusses publishers losing monetizable traffic as agents use their content, but does not highlight publishers seeking human visitors while blocking agents acting for those visitors.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the current model doesn't survive contact with agents, and that's not a bad thing. The web's ad economy was built on a very specific assumption: a human with eyeballs and attention sits in front of a page, and you can interrupt that attention and sell it. An agent doesn't have attention. You can't interrupt it. You can't make it look at a banner. It goes to a page, extracts what it needs, and leaves. So the impression, which was the atomic unit of the whole business, basically evaporates.

What people get wrong, though, is assuming that means the value disappears. The value was never really in the impression. It was in the intent. Someone searching for a hotel in Lisbon, or comparing two laptops, that's where the money always was. Agents don't eliminate intent, they concentrate it. An agent acting for you knows exactly what you want, with far more precision than any cookie ever did, because you told it. So the question becomes: who gets paid for serving that intent, and how?

I think you end up with a few things happening at once. First, publishers and sites stop giving content away for free to agents the way they gave it to crawlers. The bargain with search was "index me, send me traffic, I'll monetize the traffic." Agents break that bargain because they consume and don't send the human back. So you'll see metering, licensing, paid access, some kind of economic layer where the agent or the company behind it pays for what it reads. That's a transition from an attention economy to something closer to a transaction economy.

Second, the advertising that does survive moves up a level. If my agent is going to choose between three restaurants, merchants will want influence over that choice, and there will be enormous pressure to sell it. And I think that's the part we should be really careful about. An agent that quietly takes payment to steer my decisions isn't my agent anymore. The trust relationship is the whole product. So I'd actually bet that the winning agents are the ones that refuse that, and they'll be paid directly by the user or through transparent transaction fees, not by hidden placement.

Third, there's a lot of the web that was only ever ad-supported because there was no other way to charge. A lot of that content was thin, made for the algorithm, not for the reader. Agents are pretty good at ignoring that. So some of it just goes away, and honestly, the web gets a little better.

So in short: the display-ad-funded open web shrinks, intent gets more valuable not less, and the fight over the next decade is really about whether agents stay loyal to the people they represent or get captured the way the browser and the feed got captured. I'm more optimistic than most people, but it's not guaranteed. It depends on choices people are making right now.

r001.rationale: It says intent is valuable and merchants may pay to influence agent choices, but does not identify advertising as an efficient mechanism for differential pricing.

r002.rationale: It explains that agents lack human attention, cannot be interrupted by banners, and make the impression-based model evaporate.

r003.rationale: It says publishers may meter or license agent access because agents consume content without returning human traffic, but does not highlight publishers blocking agents while seeking human visitors.

astra-6.text:
I think it changes a pretty fundamental assumption behind advertising on the web: that the person consuming the information is also seeing the ad. If an agent is doing the browsing for you, those two things come apart. You can get the value of a website without ever visiting it yourself, and that creates a real question about how the people producing that information get paid.

But I wouldn’t jump from that to saying advertising disappears. There’s still a business trying to reach a customer, and there’s still a customer trying to find something. What changes is where that interaction happens. Does the advertising move to the interface where you talk to your agent? Do websites get paid for providing information or completing a transaction? I think we’ll see experimentation across those models.

The important tension is trust. You want your agent to recommend something because it’s right for you. If it recommends something because someone paid for that placement, you need to understand that. How we handle that tension will shape both the business model and how willing people are to delegate decisions.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses advertising and possible payment models but does not describe web advertising as an efficient mechanism for differential pricing.

r002.rationale: It says agents can browse without the human seeing the ad or visiting the website, challenging advertising’s reliance on human attention.

r003.rationale: It raises how websites get paid when agents access their information, but does not identify publishers’ conflict between seeking human visitors and blocking agents acting for them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it changes the relationship between attention and intent. Today, a lot of the web is funded by showing ads to people as they browse. If an agent does that browsing for you, it might visit a hundred pages and come back with one answer. You never see those pages, so the advertising model behind them becomes harder to sustain.

But the commercial intent is still there. If you ask an agent to help you buy something, that’s valuable to a business. The question is whether businesses pay to influence the agent’s recommendation, or whether the agent is paid by you and acts entirely in your interest. There’s a real trust issue there: why did it recommend this product?

And then there’s the question of who pays the people producing the information the agent relies on. You could imagine more subscriptions, referral fees, or payments for access to content. I don’t think there’s one obvious replacement for advertising. But agents put pressure on the assumption that, to get something useful from the web, a human has to visit a page and give it their attention.

r001.rationale: It discusses advertising and commercial intent, but does not identify web advertising as an efficient way to charge different prices to different users.

r002.rationale: It explains that agents may browse many pages and return one answer the human never sees, putting pressure on advertising’s reliance on human attention and page visits.

r003.rationale: It raises how information producers might get paid, but does not describe publishers wanting human visitors while blocking agents acting for those humans.
